title: On the formation of κ-carbides in low-density steels
abstract: Abstract This work aims to clarify the fundamental precipitation mechanisms in the Fe–Al–Mn–C system, spanning from atomic-level processes to the overall mechanical response. A multiscale characterization approach, including high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, atom probe tomography, and synchrotron X-ray diffraction, was combined to characterize the evolution of κ-carbides during aging, providing atomic-level insights into their formation. This enabled the analysis of carbide size, morphology, interparticle spacing, and volume fraction at different stages of aging. Tensile and hardness tests on samples aged at 550 ℃ for different times were performed to correlate macroscale mechanical properties with the nanoscale κ-carbides. The results show that spinodal decomposition occurs throughout the 8 h of aging, forming solute-rich regions. In contrast, the formation of κ-carbides begins in the solute-rich areas through short-range ordering in the early stages of aging, i.e., within 30 min at 550 ℃, and both the fraction and size increase with longer aging times. After 2.5 h of aging, the fraction and lattice parameter of the κ-carbides saturate and stop increasing. The yield strength and hardness follow the same trend as the κ-carbide fraction, with a steep increase in the initial stages of aging, up to 2.5 h, reaching 925 MPa and 360 HV, and then saturating after 2.5 h. This work provides a clear mechanistic understanding of the underlying strengthening mechanisms and the resulting mechanical behavior.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels are increasingly recognized as high-performance structural materials because of their excellent strength-ductility balance and lower density [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ]. A key feature controlling the mechanical response of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels is the phase evolution that occurs during isothermal aging. The current understanding of κ-carbide formation can be described as a sequence of coupled processes. First, the supersaturated austenite matrix undergoes spinodal decomposition, producing periodic chemical modulations along the elastically soft < 100 > directions, with Al- and C-enriched regions forming alongside solute-depleted regions [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. As aging proceeds, solute partitioning increases the amplitude of this compositional modulation. Within the solute-rich regions, short-range ordering (SRO) promotes the local arrangement of Al and C atoms toward the ordered κ-carbide structure [ 12 ]. In this structure, Al atoms occupy the corner positions of the unit cell, Fe and Mn atoms occupy the face positions, and C atoms occupy the body-centered octahedral interstitial sites [ 1 ]. With further ordering, coherent κ-carbide domains form within the austenite matrix, typically preserving a cube-on-cube orientation relationship and a low lattice misfit with the surrounding γ phase [ 9 ,  13 ]. Thus, spinodal decomposition provides the chemical modulation, solute partitioning enriches the κ-carbide-forming regions, and SRO enables the transition toward ordered κ-carbide formation.

Multiple studies also highlight how alloying elements influence this process: Vanadium [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ] and titanium [ 14 ] tend to form competing carbides that hinder κ-carbide growth, whereas silicon [ 15 ,  16 – 17 ] can speed up formation kinetics. Chromium (Cr) and Cr/Mo [ 14 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ] addition in the austenitic Fe–Mn-Al-C alloys suppress the precipitation of coarse Mn-rich κ-carbides on the grain boundaries .  Despite these insights, the detailed mechanisms and kinetic limits of these concurrent processes still need further clarification.

At aging temperatures ranging from 450 to 650 °C, chemical modulation promotes homogeneous precipitation of κ-carbides [ 25 ]. When the aging temperature exceeds 650 °C and reaches up to 800 °C, intergranular κ-carbides nucleate heterogeneously at the γ/γ boundaries [ 23 ,  26 ]. These intergranular κ-carbides exhibit faster growth kinetics in comparison with intragranular carbides and, as a result, attain a larger size [ 27 ]. Recently, it was found that grain boundary engineering treatment tailors κ-carbides to suppress intergranular and promote intragranular nanoprecipitates for strengthening [ 28 ].

Previous studies from the authors have focused on the microstructure-property correlation in such alloys and the correlation between mechanical properties and the size of κ-carbides [ 29 ,  30 ] .  The formation of the κ-carbides leads to precipitation hardening of the steel caused by interaction between the κ-carbides and the mobile dislocations during deformation, specifically from dislocation shearing, enabled by low lattice misfit (< 3%) and near-perfect coherency [ 31 ,  32 ]. In addition, solid solution hardening plays an important role as a strengthening mechanism due to the high contents of C, Mn, and Al [ 33 ].

The objective of this work is to elucidate the fundamental precipitation mechanisms in the Fe–Al–Mn–C system, from the atomic scale to the macroscopic mechanical response, by capturing the very early stages of precipitation and subsequently monitoring the evolution of precipitate size, fraction, and distribution, thereby linking the microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior. Here, this multiscale strategy is implemented by combining in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction during thermal treatment, to follow the evolution of the κ-carbide superlattice peak intensity, which serves as a relative indicator of ordered κ-carbide formation in the bulk, with TEM and APT analyses that provide nanoscale insight into the decomposition pathways, κ-carbide precipitation mechanisms and precipitate size distributions. The novelty of the present work lies in resolving, for the same Fe–Mn–Al–C alloy and aging treatment, the different temporal evolution of spinodal compositional modulation and ordered κ-carbide formation. While κ-carbide precipitation in low-density steels has been widely studied, the relative timing of chemical partitioning, short-range ordering, κ-carbide ordering, and mechanical strengthening remains insufficiently clarified. The present results show that compositional modulation continues to evolve during prolonged aging, whereas the κ-carbide superlattice signal and lattice parameter approach a plateau after approximately 2.5 h. This provides a mechanistic basis for linking early-stage ordering, nanoscale κ-carbide formation, and the resulting hardness, tensile strength, and work-hardening response.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
A Fe-28Mn-8.9Al-0.9C (wt.%) steel was selected for this study. The cast ingots were reheated to 1200 °C and hot-rolled in seven passes to a final thickness of 5 mm, with a total reduction ratio of 65%. After the last rolling pass, the sheets were quenched directly in water to prevent the formation of intergranular κ-carbides. Samples were cut from the sheets and aged in a muffle furnace in a sand bath under precise temperature and time control. The selected aging conditions and sample names are given below in Table  1 .
 Table 1 The names of the aged samples are based on the aging treatment conditions Name Aging temperature (°C) Aging time (h) NA – – 550_0.5 550 0.5 550_1 550 1 550_2.5 550 2.5 550_8 550 8

The aging temperature and time were chosen according to the literature review and hardness measurements. Aging at 550 °C was selected based on the hardness response as a function of aging time at this temperature. Higher or lower aging temperatures would challenge the control of κ-carbides precipitation in large-scale production lines. After aging, the pieces were cooled in air, and smaller samples were cut so that the section perpendicular to the transverse direction (TD) of rolling could be observed in the microscope. Hence, the studied samples were aged at 550 °C for 0.5 to 8 h, during which the maximum hardness was measured (peak aging condition).

For the TEM analysis, samples were prepared by mechanical grinding to a thickness of 100 μm and further thinned by electrolytic polishing in a perchloric acid solution at room temperature. A Jeol JEM-2200FS, 200 kV field emission TEM was used. Further TEM analysis was performed using a Thermo-Fischer Talos F200i field-emission TEM, operating at 200 kV.

An FEI Quanta TM 450-FEG-SEM was used for the scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The voltage was 20 kV, with a final aperture size of 50 μm and a spot size of 5, corresponding to a probe current of ~ 2.4 nA. The working distance was selected in the range of 10–15 μm. The imaging mode for the SEM was backscatter electron (BSE). For the transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) analysis, the same TEM samples were placed on a specific holder with a tilt toward the detector of − 30°. The working distance was 5 mm, and the step size used for the scan was 6 nm. The resulting patterns were acquired on a hexagonal scan grid by a Hikari detector operated with EDAX TSL–OIM-Data Collection version 7.3 software. The corresponding orientation data were post-processed with EDAX-TSL-OIM-Data Analysis version 7.3.1. software using the following grain definition: misorientation with neighboring grains higher than 15°, a minimum number of points per grain was 8, and a confidence index (CI) larger than 0.1. The raw data were post-processed in two steps to reassign the dubiously indexed points using the (i) grain confidence index standardization and (ii) neighbor orientation correlation procedure, and the number of changed points did not exceed 0.5%.

In situ annealing at the synchrotron XRD facility was performed to monitor the evolution of the precipitates. The tests were performed at the P21.2 beamline at PETRA III in Hamburg, Germany. The setup had a TS1500 Linkam furnace in transmission mode, with four VAREX XRD4343CT detector panels spaced approximately 1760 mm apart. The beam energy was 53 keV (corresponding to a wavelength of ~ 0.2339 Å). Each point was exposed to the X-ray beam for 1 s. The X-ray beam-spot size was about 1 × 1 mm 2 . The detector position was calibrated with a LaB 6  NIST SRM 660a standard crystal using the GSAS-2 [ 34 ]. The 2D diffraction images were integrated along the entire azimuthal range, covering approximately an azimuthal range of about 84 degrees per panel, and the diffractograms were batch-fitted in GSAS-II to obtain the peak position, full width at half maximum (FWHM), and the integrated intensity of the diffraction peaks, along with the standard uncertainties of the fitted parameters obtained from the least-squares peak-profile fitting.

The atom probe instruments used in this study belong to the CAMECA local electrode atom probe (LEAP) 5000XR series. All APT experiments were conducted in laser mode at 40 K with a laser pulse energy of 30 pJ, a pulse frequency of 200 kHz, and a detection rate of 1.5%. The IVAS 6.3 software was utilized for data reconstruction, analysis, and visualization. APT needle-shaped specimens were prepared in a dual-beam SEM/FIB FEI Helios Nanolab 600i instrument. Before preparing site-specific, grain boundary (GB)-containing samples, electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) measurements were conducted on the bulk sample to identify sites of interest.

For the tensile tests, sub-size samples with a gauge length of 25 mm were cut from the hot-rolled sheets parallel to the rolling direction, in accordance with the ASTM E8 standard geometry. The strain rate for the tensile tests was 10 –3  s −1 , with three specimens tested per condition. The results were reproducible. Finally, Vickers hardness tests were performed using a DuraVista-40 Hardness Tester with a 10 kg load (HV10), with twelve indents made per sample.

sections.heading: Initial microstructure before aging
paragraphs: The NA material was studied in SEM and TEM, as shown in Fig.  1 . The microstructure consists of austenite grains with annealing twins (Supplementary material–Figures  S1  and  S2 ). The shape of the austenite grains is equiaxed due to the completion of the recrystallization process after the hot rolling. TEM analysis has shown that no κ-carbides have formed during hot-rolling, neither inside the grains nor at grain boundaries and triple junctions. Figure 1 Microstructure of hot-rolled non-aged steel.  a  General SEM view showing the austenite grains and annealing twins (AT).  b  TEM image of an area containing an annealing twin.

sections.heading: κ-carbide formation and growth
paragraphs: The precipitation of κ-carbides was studied using TEM in grains with a [100] zone axis. At the selected aging temperature, the grains do not coarsen [ 30 ]. As precipitation is the only observed microstructural change, it is concluded that the primary hardening mechanisms is solid solution strengthening and precipitation hardening through the growth of κ-carbides. Figure  2  shows dark field (DF) images, inverse fast Fourier transformation (IFFT) images and selected area electron diffraction patterns (SAEDPs) for samples aged 0.5 h, 1 h, 2.5 h, and 8 h. For the DF images, the (100) κ  diffraction spot was used. It is observed that the κ-carbides are homogeneously distributed inside the interior of the grains. IFTT images are utilized to study the morphology, size, and interparticle spacing of the κ-carbides at higher magnification. In these images, the color intensity corresponds to the intensity of the superlattice reflections. The atoms of κ-carbides appear white, while the austenite matrix is black. No clear interface between the carbides and the matrix is observed; instead, a smooth transition over distance is observed, and the atoms producing intermediate intensities are shown in blue. For more information on the IFFT image processing, the reader is referred to the Supplementary material – Figure  S3 . For the initial stages of aging, carbides appear as fine particles distributed in the austenite matrix. The size of the κ-carbides increased from 1 nm after 0.5 h aging to 3 nm after 8 h. The average diameter of the κ-carbides calculated after 0.5 h, 1h, 2.5h and 8h of aging is presented in Table  2 . For calculating carbide size, 200 particles were measured per sample. Figure 2 Dark field (DF) TEM images using the (010)κ diffraction spots show the distribution of the carbides inside the austenite grains after different aging treatments. The IFFT HR-TEM images are used to observe the morphology and size of the κ-carbides. At the same time, the SAED patterns offer crystallographic information for the κ-carbides and the austenite matrix. Table 2 The calculated diameter with standard deviation and relative accuracy of the κ-carbides for each aged sample Sample Average diameter (nm) 550_0.5 1.04 (± 0.29) 550_1 1.26 (± 0.33) 550_2.5 2.40 (± 0.6) 550_8 2.98 (± 0.9)

Finally, from the SAEDPs in Fig.  2 c, f, l, o, the superlattice diffraction spots from the ordered κ-carbides are visible in all aged samples (marked with yellow). The (010) and (110) superlattice diffraction spots of the carbides are typical for ordered structures, confirming the cube-on-cube orientation relationship with the austenite matrix: [100] κ  // [100] γ  and [010] κ  // [010] γ , with a lattice misfit of less than 3% [ 2 ]. In the SAEDPs taken from samples aged less than 2.5 h, the (110)κ diffraction spot has very low intensity, whereas in the 8-h-aged sample, the intensity of the specific diffraction spot has increased significantly. It has been reported that the ordering of C atoms at the body center site of the ordered L1 2  structure is responsible for such an intensity difference [ 10 ].

The spinodal decomposition and ordering are concomitant, and diffraction satellites around the diffraction spots originate from fluctuations in the chemical composition, as shown in the diffraction patterns and the line profiles in Fig.  3 , which corresponds to the SAED pattern of the 550_8 sample (Fig.  2 o). Figure 3 a  SAED pattern of the 550_8 sample,  b  Enlarged image of the (220)γ spot where the line profiles 1 and 2 were taken.  c  drawing of the SAED pattern where the Miller indices are given. The L1 2  superlattice diffraction spots are given in yellow, while the austenite matrix diffraction spots with the satellite diffractions are drawn in blue color.  d  line profile of line 1,  e  line profile of line 2.

Specifically, the satellite diffraction spots are clearly visible at this stage of aging. In the other samples, aged for 0.5–2.5 h, the satellite diffraction spots cannot be distinguished due to the small modulation wavelength. These diffraction satellites around the diffraction and incident spots originate from fluctuations in the C concentration along the < 100 > direction. They indicate modulation of solute elements along the [100] and [010] directions, which also corresponds to the findings of Choo et al. [ 10 ]. On the other hand, the presence of the L1 2  superlattice diffraction spots originates from the concurrent ordering of Fe and Al [ 3 ]. An indexed drawing of the SAED pattern of the [100] zone axis with the superlattice diffractions (yellow) and the satellite diffraction spots (blue) is shown in Fig.  3 c.

Additionally, the intensity line profiles of the satellite diffractions as shown in Fig.  3 d, e indicate that three different compositions are present in the microstructure: the central peak (main diffraction spot) and the two sidebands (satellite diffraction spots) on the left and right, which correspond to different chemical compositions, thereby changing the lattice parameter of the austenite matrix slightly.

The occurrence of spinodal decomposition is also apparent as sidebands in the X-ray diffraction patterns; some indicative X-ray diffraction patterns at different annealing times are shown in Fig.  4 . Specifically, sidebands are observed on both sides of each austenite peak, similar to the satellites shown in the SAED patterns. The sidebands on the left (= at lower 2θ from the central, FCC main peaks) correspond to larger lattice parameters and thus to κ-carbides with higher Al and C content. In contrast, the right sidebands (= at higher 2θ from the central, main FCC peaks) correspond to smaller lattice parameters and austenite regions depleted of Al and C. At the initial stages of aging, the sidebands are barely visible, and their intensity increases considerably with aging. In addition to the sidebands, superlattice diffraction peaks appear with aging time, corresponding to the formation of κ-carbides. Figure 4 Synchrotron X-ray diffraction patterns for the aged samples, showing the formation of sidebands, left and right to the main FCC peaks, with increasing aging time. Supperlattice diffraction peaks also appear with aging time, as denoted with arrows.

sections.heading: Spinodal decomposition and carbide formation mechanism
paragraphs: Quantitative determination of the κ-carbide fraction using methods such as Rietveld refinement is challenging due to the presence of spinodal decomposition and the complexity of the diffraction profiles. Therefore, the evolution of integrated peak intensities was used as a qualitative indicator to assess the mechanism of κ-carbide formation and its relation to spinodal decomposition.

To distinguish between compositional modulation and ordered precipitation, the integrated intensities of the (220) sidebands and the (110) superlattice peaks are tracked in Fig.  5 . While both intensities increase during the initial stages of aging, indicating concurrent spinodal decomposition and κ-carbide formation, they diverge thereafter. The saturation of the superlattice peak intensity after 2.5 h suggests that the ordering transformation is arrested. In contrast, the sideband intensity continues to rise linearly up to 8 h, indicating that the amplitude of the compositional modulation (chemical partitioning) continues to increase even after the ordered carbide fraction has stabilized. It should be noted that the superlattice peak intensity is used here to track the relative evolution of κ-carbide ordering under identical experimental conditions, rather than as a direct quantitative measure of phase fraction, since reliable phase-fraction refinement is hindered by the overlap between matrix and κ-carbide reflections. This decoupling confirms that κ-carbides form within solute-rich regions generated by spinodal decomposition but are governed by different kinetic limits. The increase in sideband intensity is also related to the coherency strain fields between the κ-carbides and the matrix, as well as to elastic distortion caused by their growth. Hence, the κ-carbides grow larger, increasing the strain field and the elastic fields, which in turn influence the intensity of the sidebands. Additionally, as reported by Elkot et al. [ 35 ,  36 ], during the coarsening of the κ-carbides, the periodicity is enhanced, resulting in periodic strain modulation. Figure 5 The evolution of the integrated intensity of the left sideband of the (220) FCC reflection and the (110) κ-carbide superlattice diffraction peak, calculated from the in situ XRD investigation with increasing annealing time at 550 ℃.

On the other hand, concerning the κ-carbides, the change in the lattice parameter was calculated based on the position of the superlattice diffraction peaks. As it is shown in Fig.  7 a, the lattice parameter of the κ-carbides saturates after 2.5 h of aging, indicating that they reach the expected stoichiometry, i.e., (Fe, Mn) 3 AlC. These results suggest that carbon acts as a critical 'bottleneck' for the precipitation of κ-carbide in the investigated Fe–28Mn–8.9Al–0.9C (wt.%) steel. This limitation is rooted in the stoichiometry of the κ-carbide, which possesses an E21 crystal structure with the chemical formula (Fe, Mn) 3 AlC. In this structure, a single carbon atom must occupy the central interstitial site for every three metal atoms (Fe, Mn) and one aluminum atom. Quantitatively, the alloy contains 3.69 at.% carbon, which is significantly lower than the available 16.26 at.% aluminum and 25.13 at.% manganese. Given the 1:1 atomic ratio required between C and Al for stoichiometric κ-carbide, carbon is the limiting reagent. Calculations based on these atomic fractions indicate that the 3.69 at.% of carbon can support a maximum theoretical κ-carbide volume fraction of approximately 18.5%, leaving a substantial surplus of Al and Mn in the matrix. This chemical limitation is directly supported by the in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction data, which shows that both the integrated intensity of the (110) superlattice peaks and the κ-carbide lattice parameter saturate after 2.5 h of aging at 550 °C. The stabilization of the lattice parameter at this juncture suggests the precipitates have reached their final (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC stoichiometry and that carbon availability may limit further development of ordered κ-carbides. Notably, while the ordering transformation (the formation of κ-carbides) ceases at 2.5 h, the intensity of the sidebands—which represents the amplitude of chemical partitioning during spinodal decomposition—continues to increase up to 8 h. This divergence confirms that while solute elements continue to partition into rich and depleted regions, these solute-rich areas can no longer undergo the ordering transformation into κ-carbides due to the absence of sufficient carbon atoms. At around 2.5 h, the precipitation process transitions from forming new superlattice structures to the growth of existing κ-carbides via coalescence. The observed decrease in the κ-carbide lattice parameter (Fig.  7 a) is consistent with that reported in [ 41 ]. In this work, APT is combined with density functional theory (DFT) to explain that Al depletion of coherent k-carbide in a γ-matrix occurs concurrently with reduced C content in the precipitates. Specifically, κ-carbides showed depletion of both C and Al compared to the ideal stoichiometric composition. The aluminum depletion was explained by manganese atoms occupying aluminum sites (Mn γ Al  anti-site defects) only when carbon vacancies were present nearby. DFT calculations showed that the manganese anti-sites have very high formation energies when carbon sites are fully occupied, making them unlikely to form. Nevertheless, when carbon vacancies are present adjacent to potential anti-site locations, the formation energy drops dramatically, making manganese anti-sites energetically favorable. The lower carbon at.% in the studied alloy leads to more vacancies and promotes Mn γ Al  anti-site defects. Additionally, the compressive elastic strain from the coherent κ/γ interface promotes these anti-site defects, as their formation energies drop notably under volumetric compression. The strain shifts the Al-C interaction from repulsion to attraction; however, the presence of carbon vacancies alleviates this constraint. The stabilization of the lattice parameter at 2.5 h probably indicates stoichiometric saturation, meaning that the interstitial sites within the (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC unit cells are fully occupied, halting further carbon diffusion and structural change. Figure 7 a  The evolution of the lattice constant of the κ-carbides, as has been calculated from the position of the superlattice reflection peaks.  b  IFFT image of the 550_8 sample; the red dots correspond to atoms contributing to the main diffraction spots, while green dots correspond to atoms contributing to the superlattice diffraction spots.

Figure  7 b and its insert, which is a magnification of the area inside the square, is an inverse fast Fourier transformation (IFFT) image (Supplementary materials—Figure S4), where the red dots correspond to the atoms that contribute to the main diffraction spot (i.e., γ + κ), while the green dots correspond to the atoms that contribute to the superlattice diffraction spots. From this image of the 550_8 sample, it is evident that the κ-carbides are superlattice structures formed homogeneously in the austenite matrix, maintaining near-perfect coherency and preserving the orientation relationship (001)κ // (001)γ.

Figure  8  shows the analysis of an APT top prepared from samples aged at 550°C for 2.5 and 8 h. The 3D atomic maps of Fe, Mn, Al, and C are displayed. Frequency distribution analysis is shown in the plot on the right side of Fig.  8 . In this analysis, the observed distribution of elemental concentration in blocks of 100 atoms is compared with the binomial distribution representing ideal randomness. The insert table presents the values of the normalized chi-squared, µ. Complete randomness renders µ = 0, while µ = 1 means perfect association of atoms [ 42 ]. Low µ values are observed for all elements. These low values are due to the small size and the dispersity of κ-carbides. Additionally, both κ-carbides and the matrix contain a mixture of the alloying elements. The values of µ increase by 0.05–0.06 for Fe, Al, and C as the aging increases from 2.5 h to 8 h, indicating increased partitioning. In contrast, Mn partitioning does not change significantly, as reflected by the slight change in µ value. Figure 8 APT 3D atomic maps of Fe, Mn, Al, C of the 2.5 h and 8h aged samples. The plots on the right side of the figure show the frequency distribution analysis of Fe, Mn, Al and C with the µ values shown in the inset table. The probability p-values measured for all elements are < 0.0001.

The 3D atomic maps of the 8-h-aged sample show precipitation of κ-carbides and chemical partitioning between them and the matrix. It can be observed that between 2.5 and 8 h of aging, the partitioning of C is more pronounced than that of the other elements, and the zones with increased C concentration (carbides) are more distinctly visible.

Figure  9  shows a section from the 3D volume render of C + Al for the 2.5-h- and 8-h-aged samples. This visualization reveals the precipitation of κ-carbides in two orthogonal directions, as shown by the black-dashed lines. This appearance is a result of the precipitation of κ-carbides along < 001 > directions. To visualize the morphology of the κ-carbides and perform proximity histogram analysis, interfaces were defined using iso-concentration surfaces at C ≥ 7 at.%. Given that these precipitates emerge via spinodal decomposition and exhibit a gradient interface, this specific threshold was selected to delineate the regions of significant carbon enrichment—nearly double the bulk composition of 3.69 at.%—identifying the zones where the ordering transformation into the E2 1  structure is most advanced. Figure  9 c and Fig.  9 e show the proximity histograms of the interfaces in Fig.  9 a and d, respectively. These histograms show the average C composition across these interfaces and reveal the chemical partitioning of C. The absence of a sharp interface in the APT data reveals a continuous compositional gradient between the precipitates and the matrix, directly corroborating the smooth transition observed in the IFFT HR-TEM images. This lack of discrete phase separation further aligns with the synchrotron XRD results, where the presence of sidebands indicates a continuous modulation of solute elements rather than a sudden shift in lattice parameters. Figure 9 a  3D atomic map of C overlayed with interfaces created at C ≥ 7 at.% iso-concentration surfaces.  b  A section in the 3D volume render of Al + C. Regions with high Al + C concentration highlight κ-carbides.  c  Proximity histogram of the interfaces created at C ≥ 7 at..%.

It has to be noted that APT compositional measurements are subject to several sources of uncertainty. It is expected that the local magnification effect originating from the difference in evaporation field between the κ-carbides and the matrix will broaden the compositional gradient observed in the proximity histograms [ 43 ]. Additionally, C ions are likely to go undetected due to multiple hit events [ 44 ]. Lastly, the selection of the iso-concentration surface threshold influences the C concentration in the carbides, especially due to the small size [ 45 ] and the absence of a sharp interface in spinodal decomposition. Hence, it is likely that the reported C concentration values are underestimates. Nevertheless, the conclusions drawn here rely on relative compositional differences rather than absolute compositions and are therefore not critical to our conclusions.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The Vickers hardness results are shown in Fig.  10 a. The initial NA sample exhibits a hardness of 287 HV. After aging at 550 °C, the hardness increases with aging. Initially, the hardness increases relatively rapidly, while beyond 2.5 h, the rate of increase becomes significantly lower. Figure 10 a  The Vickers hardness profile for the aged samples; the error bars correspond to the standard deviation observed on 12 measurements per sample.  b  The engineering stress–strain curves of the aged samples. Two out of the three curves measured are given in this diagram with straight and dashed lines.  c  The work-hardening rate as a function of the true strain for three aging conditions.

The engineering stress–strain curves for each condition are shown in Fig.  10 b. As observed from the figure and from Table  3 , the yield strength (YS) is increasing with increasing aging time, alongside the ultimate tensile strength (UTS). On the other hand, the total elongation at failure (TE) is decreasing significantly. The values presented in Table  3  are the average of three tensile tests per condition, and the standard deviation is provided in brackets.
 Table 3 The engineering stress–strain values are provided in the table Aging time (h) YS (MPa) UTS (MPa) TE (%) 0.5 733 (± 15) 1019 (± 5) 77 (± 5) 1 838 (± 5) 1036 (± 5) 72 (± 5) 2.5 926 (± 5) 1070 (± 5) 66 (± 5) 8 1015 (± 5) 1141 (± 10) 49 (± 5) The values presented are the average of three tests and the standard deviation is given

Figure  10 c shows the work hardening rate as a function of true strain. For all three samples, the work hardening rate increases after a plastic strain of 0.03, reaching a maximum value of about 1930 MPa at a true strain of 0.29 in the 550_1 sample, 1755 MPa at 0.26 in the 550_2.5 sample, and 1680 MPa at 0.23 in the 550_8 sample. The work hardening rate generally decreases with longer aging times, with a more noticeable decline during the early aging period from 1 to 2.5 h.

Four stages are distinguished in the work-hardening rate curves in similar alloys [ 46 ]. Initially, dislocations glide over long distances due to low dislocation density, with minimal accumulation and dislocation growth driven mainly by dynamic recovery [ 47 ]. This causes a drop in work hardening rate [ 48 ,  49 – 50 ]. In this stage, κ-carbide particles partially interact with dislocations, acting as obstacles and raising yield strength [ 51 ].

In the second stage, the work-hardening rate recovers as dislocations shear κ-carbides, reducing their size, thereby facilitating further shearing and suppressing cross-slip. The process promotes dislocation planar slip, aided by κ-carbide interactions and SRO destruction and prevents dislocation annihilation [ 46 ].

After the work-hardening rate recovers, a plateau appears as strain increases, due to the softening effect of the κ-carbides [ 32 ,  52 ]. At high-strain levels, austenite grains exhibit orientation differences due to planar slip microstructures. Slip bands form a Taylor lattice, with domain boundaries [ 53 ,  54 ], while high strain enhances the rotation of Taylor lattice domains, creating more boundaries and microbands [ 30 ], leading to grain subdivision, slight misorientations, and Hall–Petch strengthening. Figure  11  shows the formation of Taylor lattices in the deformed 550_8 sample, after the tensile test, in bright field (Fig.  11 a) and dark field (Fig.  11 b) TEM mode. The domains and κ-carbides are visible in the selected grain. TKD maps of the same grain are given in Fig.  11 c and d. The inverse pole figure (IPF) map shows misorientations within the grain, as indicated by color changes, while the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map shows higher angle misorientations in green, corresponding to domain boundaries. Figure 11 a  Bright field TEM image of the deformed 550_8 sample after the tensile test.  b  Dark field TEM image of the same area.  c  IPF TKD map of an area of the same grain.  d  KAM TKD map of the same area.

With the strain increasing further in the fourth stage, the dislocation cross-slip characteristic becomes more pronounced, and the work hardening rate drops steadily in the final stage; dynamic recovery should be the leading factor, resulting from the gradual decrease in the rate of dislocation density evolution [ 53 ]. The high work-hardening rate and its slight decrease indicate that the work-hardening capability remains high.

sections.heading: Microstructure – properties correlation
paragraphs: Finally, Fig.  12  correlates the aging time with the mechanical properties. Both hardness and yield strength reach a plateau after 2.5 h of aging. Figure 12 Correlation between the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and Vickers hardness with the aging time.

Regarding spinodal decomposition, it was shown that the composition wavelength, as indicated by the position of the sidebands in Fig.  6 a, increases significantly for the first 2.5 h of aging, followed by a more moderate increase. On the other hand, the amplitude, as indicated by the intensity of the sidebands in Fig.  5 a, increases almost linearly with aging time, augmenting periodic internal coherency stresses that effectively impede dislocation motion. Although the shift of the diffraction sidebands observed in synchrotron X-ray diffraction confirms a simultaneous coarsening of the modulation wavelength, macroscopic hardening is fundamentally driven by amplitude growth [ 55 ,  56 ]. In accordance with Kato’s model [ 57 ], the yield stress scales linearly with amplitude and remains independent of wavelength.

Regarding the effect of κ-carbides, Kim et al. [ 32 ] showed that κ-carbides are sheared by dislocations because of their coherency with the austenite matrix, which strengthens the material even at precipitate sizes around 40 nm. These carbides hinder dislocation movement by blocking their glide through the austenite matrix. Additionally, larger carbide sizes lead to shorter interparticle spacings, thereby reducing dislocation glide paths and enhancing yield strength. In this study, it is observed that κ-carbides begin forming in solute-rich regions, and after about 2.5 h, their lattice parameter stabilizes. Their size increases through coarsening and coalescence, but does not reach 40 nm as reported by Kim et al. [ 32 ]. This means that the size of the κ-carbides after 8 h of aging is too small for Orowan looping to occur, while the interparticle spacing decreases as aging progresses. The shearing of the κ-carbides has been demonstrated in previous works [ 29 ,  31 ,  32 ]. The microstructure–property relationship can be described as a sequence of coupled processes. During early aging, spinodal decomposition produces Al- and C-enriched regions that promote short-range ordering and coherent κ-carbide formation. The rapid increase in the κ-carbide ordering signal, together with increasing carbide size and decreasing interparticle spacing, explains the steep rise in hardness and yield strength up to approximately 2.5 h. At longer aging times, the κ-carbide superlattice signal and lattice parameter approach is a plateau, whereas the sideband intensity continues to increase, suggesting continued compositional modulation and/or increasing coherency strain. Thus, the mechanical response arises from the combined effects of coherent κ-carbide shearing, interparticle spacing reduction and spinodal modulation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The current work focuses on the spinodal decomposition and the formation of κ-carbides through short-range ordering in an austenitic low-density steel, and how they affect the mechanical properties. The experiments combined high-resolution TEM and in situ heating experiments in a synchrotron XRD facility, along with APT, to study the precipitation mechanisms from the very early stages of aging. It can be concluded that: Concerning the spinodal decomposition, spontaneous chemical partitioning of aluminum and carbon takes place at the initial stages of aging, along the elastic < 100 > directions, as shown in the selected area diffraction patterns. The modulation wavelength increases with aging time, at a faster rate until 2.5 h of aging, and at a slower rate for the rest of the aging treatment. On the contrary, the amplitude, as is indicated by the intensity of the sidebands, increases almost linearly with aging time. This means that the chemical modulation and separation of solute-rich and solute-depleted areas continue throughout the entire aging process. Concerning the formation of κ-carbides, superlattice reflections in selected area diffraction patterns and synchrotron XRD indicate that short-range ordering occurs concurrently with the spinodal decomposition. The intensity of the superlattice reflections of the κ-carbides saturates after 2.5 h of aging, similarly to their lattice parameter. This means that the ordering transformation stops at this stage, and the observed increase in carbide size is attributed to coalescence of the κ-carbides. The saturation in the ordering transformation is driven by the lack of carbon atoms due to the lower atomic fraction. The lack of carbon atoms also explains the observed decrease in the lattice parameter of the κ-carbides, as the vacancies favor the occupation of aluminum sites by manganese atoms. Macroscopic yield strength and hardness stabilize after 2.5 h of aging, primarily due to the linear increase in spinodal modulation amplitude rather than wavelength. The strengthening mechanism involves dislocations shearing coherent κ-carbides. The size, fraction, and decreased interparticle spacing of these carbides influence the yield strength and work-hardening rate by interacting with gliding dislocations.
